title: US state capitals
subtitle: All 50 states
about: The capital of each of the 50 US states, grouped by Census region and division so neighbours are learned together. Washington, D.C. is a federal district, not a state, so it is not included.

cards.note: Its earlier Native American name, Cushnoc, meant head of the tide; Fort Western, built on the Kennebec River in 1754, still stands.
Named in 1765 to mark the new concord, or harmony, that ended a bitter boundary dispute between the towns of Rumford and Bow.
Named after the French city of Montpellier; it is the least populous state capital in the United States.
Settled by Puritans in 1630 and named after Boston in Lincolnshire, England, the hometown of colonist Isaac Johnson.
Founded in 1636 by Roger Williams, banished from Massachusetts, who named it for God's merciful Providence in giving him a haven.
Named after Hertford in England and long nicknamed the Insurance Capital of the World; Mark Twain wrote his most famous works there.
Grew from the Dutch fur trading post of Fort Orange; renamed by the English in 1664 after James, Duke of York and Albany.
Washington crossed the icy Delaware on Christmas night 1776 to defeat Hessian troops here; a bridge proclaims Trenton Makes, The World Takes.
Named after John Harris Sr., an English trader who settled beside the Susquehanna River in 1719; his son laid out the town in 1785.
Founded in 1812 as a purpose-built capital on the high banks of the Scioto River, opposite Franklinton, and named after Christopher Columbus.
A settlement of fewer than 20 people when chosen in 1847 to move the capital away from Detroit, uncomfortably close to British Canada.
A planned capital laid out in 1821; its name joins Indiana with polis, the Greek word for city.
Abraham Lincoln lived and worked here as a lawyer and politician for 24 years before the presidency; his tomb is in the city.
Built on an isthmus between Lake Mendota and Lake Monona, and named after James Madison, the fourth US president.
Early settlers called it Pig's Eye after Pierre Parrant's tavern; a missionary priest had them adopt the name of his chapel to St. Paul.
Named after the Des Moines River; the French name literally means of the monks, though its true origin is debated.
Chosen as capital in 1821 and named after Thomas Jefferson; it sits on the southern bank of the Missouri River.
Its name comes from a Kansa-Osage phrase often translated as a good place to dig potatoes; Brown v. Board of Education began here.
Founded as the village of Lancaster; renamed after the assassinated Abraham Lincoln when it was chosen as the capital in 1867.
Pronounced peer; it faces Fort Pierre across the Missouri River, an old trading post named after fur trader Pierre Chouteau Jr.
The Northern Pacific Railway named it after German chancellor Otto von Bismarck in 1873, hoping to attract German settlers and investment.
In a Dover tavern on 7 December 1787, delegates voted unanimously to make Delaware the first state to ratify the Constitution.
Congress met in its State House in 1783 and 1784, briefly making it the US capital; the Treaty of Paris was ratified there.
Patrick Henry gave his Give me liberty or give me death speech at St. John's Church in 1775; later the Confederate capital.
Sits where the Elk River meets the Kanawha; probably named after Charles Clendenin, and Daniel Boone was among its first trustees.
Named after Sir Walter Raleigh, sponsor of the lost colony of Roanoke; known as the City of Oaks for its oak-lined streets.
Laid out in 1786 as one of the first planned US cities; much of it burned in February 1865 after Sherman's army captured it.
Began as the end point of a railway line, first known simply as Terminus; largely burned during Sherman's March to the Sea in 1864.
Chosen as a halfway point between Pensacola and St. Augustine, where the legislature had alternated; its Muskogean name means old fields.
Named after Frank's Ford, a Kentucky River crossing where pioneer Stephen Frank was killed in a skirmish in 1780.
Founded in 1779 as Fort Nashborough and named after Revolutionary War general Francis Nash; Music City is home to the Grand Ole Opry.
The first capital of the Confederacy in 1861; Rosa Parks's arrest here in 1955 sparked the Montgomery bus boycott.
Named after Andrew Jackson; Union troops burned it so thoroughly in 1863 that it became known as Chimneyville.
Named after a small stone outcrop on the Arkansas River, a landmark for travellers noted by French explorer Bénard de la Harpe in 1722.
French for red stick, after a red-painted pole that French explorers found marking the boundary between two Native American peoples' lands.
Briefly incorporated as Waterloo in 1839, then renamed after Stephen F. Austin, remembered as the Father of Texas.
Settled almost overnight in the Land Run of 22 April 1889; it took over from Guthrie as the state capital in 1910.
Grew from a mining camp after four prospectors struck gold at Last Chance Gulch in 1864.
French trappers called its tree-lined river la rivière boisée, the wooded river, a landmark in the surrounding high desert.
Platted by the Union Pacific Railroad in 1867 and named after the Cheyenne people; it hosts the Cheyenne Frontier Days rodeo.
The Mile High City: a benchmark on the State Capitol steps sits exactly one mile above sea level. Named after Governor James W. Denver.
Founded by the Spanish in 1610, it is the oldest and the highest state capital in the US; its name means holy faith.
Settler Darrell Duppa chose the name for a city born from the ruins of a former civilization, the canals of the Hohokam people.
Founded by Brigham Young and Latter-day Saint pioneers in 1847 as Great Salt Lake City; the Great was dropped in 1868.
Named via the Carson River after scout Kit Carson; it boomed with the nearby Comstock Lode and had its own branch of the US Mint.
Grew around Sutter's Fort during the Gold Rush and was the western end of both the Pony Express and the first transcontinental railroad.
Its name is an anglicised form of the Hebrew shalom, meaning peace; it grew from a Methodist mission in the Willamette Valley.
Named in 1850 for its view of the Olympic Mountains; it sits at the southern end of Puget Sound.
Named after gold prospector Joe Juneau; no roads connect it to the rest of Alaska or North America, so visitors arrive by air or sea.
Its name means sheltered harbour; Iolani Palace, home of the Hawaiian monarchs, is the only royal palace on US soil.
